name: Ukraine
summary_text: Nothing about being trans is criminalised in Ukraine. Legal gender recognition exists, but the procedure is medicalised: the 2016 protocol requires a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation before documents are amended. Against that requirement stands a concrete gain — a Ukrainian court ordered changes to passports and all other documents for two trans people without requiring sterilisation.  Obtaining the diagnosis that unlocks those documents has become harder. ZMINA reported on 28 July 2026 that trans women in Ukraine now face stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers when seeking a diagnosis, and that the difficulty is documentary as much as medical, affecting both the transition procedure and border crossing. Reporting from France 24 in June 2022 already placed Ukraine's trans community in the crosshairs of the war.  Wartime procedure carries the sharpest visitor-facing risk. Gender Stream documents that since martial law began, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service, and the organisation helps with processing or reissuing documents for transgender people, including those planning to cross the border legally. Human Rights Watch reported on 15 May 2024 that cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and the often-humiliating Military Medical Commission confirmation; a Ukrainian activist described the commission's 8am to 8pm operating hours and gatekeeping that turns on a single doctor's statement.  Family recognition is now at risk in draft law. A revised Civil Code draft submitted to Parliament on 22 January 2026 would automatically annul marriages if one spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment, directly targeting trans people's family status. Trans Forum 2026, held in Kyiv in early June 2026, discussed that draft's effect on the transition procedure and whether being trans should ground an exemption from mobilisation.  Protection machinery exists but is thin. Amnesty International reported on 16 May 2013 that Ukraine's government had to legislate against discrimination and violent attacks on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity amid a pervasive climate of homophobia, and that attacks were routinely used as a pretext to deny LGBTI people the right to expression and peaceful public events. The European Parliament put the situation of transgender people in Ukraine amid the Russian invasion on the record in written question E-002018/2022 in June 2022.

sources.title: Ukrainian Civil Code (2011 amendment) and 2016 transgender procedure reform + August 2016 ruling
sources.documents: Allows transgender people who underwent surgery to change name; since Dec 2016 new IDs issued before surgery per Aug 2016 ruling ordering passport/document changes without surgery; removes 30-day psychiatric hospital and special commission permission requirements.
sources.detail: 2011 Civil Code amendment; August 2016 ruling for two transgender people; new procedure since December 2016; prior requirement: age 25+, special commission of Ministry of Healthcare, transsexuality diagnosis

name: Uruguay
summary_text: Uruguay's trans-protection regime rests on the Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law No. 19684), promulgated by the Executive in October 2018, which establishes state-guaranteed identity, health and anti-discrimination rights and directs government to ensure that trans people are treated respectfully by authorities and are not denied health services.  Legal gender recognition is administrative and based on self-declaration. Since October 2018 no surgery, hormone therapy or diagnosis has been required to change legal gender on official documents; adults have been able to change name and legal gender since October 2009, and minors may do so with parental consent under the 2018 law. Documents carry only female and male markers, even though article 4c of Law No. 19684 recognises non-binary people in its definitions.  Crimes motivated by sexual orientation or sexual identity attract enhanced penalties under article 149ter of the Penal Code, and incitement to hatred on those grounds has been prohibited since 2003. The 2004 anti-discrimination law created a permanent honorary commission empowered to investigate unlawful discriminatory conduct, including on grounds of sexual orientation and sexual identity. Non-discrimination, a ban on conversion therapy and an equal age of consent of 15 are in force, and hate-crime rules cover sexual orientation and gender identity.  Same-sex relations are legal nationwide, same-sex marriage has been legal since August 2013, and Uruguay was the first country in Latin America to recognise same-sex civil unions, in legislation signed in December 2007 granting couples who had cohabited five years or more rights equivalent to marriage. Joint adoption by same-sex couples has been permitted since September 2009, also a regional first.  Trans people in custody have the right to decide whether to be held in a men's or a women's prison. Official figures cited by the Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Prison System record 28 trans women and nine trans men among 14,965 people deprived of liberty. The director of the National Rehabilitation Institute told a parliamentary hearing that trans women are currently placed in women's prisons but that cohabitation entails a process of adaptation, and that a new women's prison at Punta de Rieles would for the first time account for the trans population; a dedicated sector for trans people was announced in July 2023 as part of a new prison planned for Montevideo.  Lethal and everyday violence against trans people persists. Joana, a 29-year-old trans woman, was shot dead in her Montevideo home on 28 July 2025; a suspect was subsequently sentenced to seven years for the murder. Studies cited in country coverage report that about two-thirds of transgender Uruguayans have been victims of physical violence and that their life expectancy is around 45 years against a national average of 77.  Discrimination in services is documented in individual cases. In May 2024 a trans health-service user, Andreina Stuart, filed a criminal complaint alleging mistreatment and discrimination at San Carlos hospital in Maldonado, after which the hospital director pledged an administrative investigation and local officials pressed for health-system updates. Beccah Rivas, a trans woman, sued the state bank BROU over discriminatory handling by a Prosegur guard and alleges the bank withheld the key camera footage; prosecutor Tania Vidal compelled the bank to produce material, and Rivas says she was dismissed after publicising the case.

sources.title: Ley Integral Para Personas Trans - Comprehensive Law for Trans Persons (Law 19,684)
sources.documents: Transgender legal status, enforcement and rights machinery: allows legal gender change with parental consent for minors, no surgery/hormones/diagnosis requirement since Oct 2018, mandates respect by authorities, housing, education, health access, 1% of scholarships, and monetary reparations for trans people persecuted during Uruguayan Dictatorship (est. ~50 people)
sources.detail: Cited as passed Oct 2018 by General Assembly 62-26 in Chamber of Representatives and 17-12 in Senate; article 4c recognizes non-binary persons in definitions but no third marker beyond female/male; Obras Sanitarias del Estado began offering jobs for trans people July 2019 in compliance; no URL visible in text
